prompt: Which list names the three types of violations of the octet rule?

choices.text: odd-electron molecules, electron-deficient molecules, and expanded valence shell molecules
odd-electron molecules, electron-deficient molecules, and molecules with double bonds
choices.why: A double bond is how atoms such as C and O in CO2 reach an octet, so it is a way of following the octet rule, not a violation.

choices.text: electron-deficient molecules, expanded valence shell molecules, and polar covalent molecules
choices.why: Polarity describes how evenly a bonding pair is shared, not how many electrons surround an atom, so a polar bond does not violate the octet rule.

choices.text: odd-electron molecules, expanded valence shell molecules, and diatomic molecules
choices.why: Many diatomic molecules, such as F2 and N2, give each atom a complete octet, so having two atoms is not a violation in itself.

explanation: The three violations of the octet rule are odd-electron molecules, electron-deficient molecules, and expanded valence shell molecules. Double bonds, polar bonds, and diatomic molecules are all compatible with the octet rule.

prompt: Some stable molecules violate the octet rule. What does this mean for the octet rule?

choices.text: The rule is still very useful; the violations are well-known exceptions.
The rule is useless, because molecules can violate it.
choices.why: Having exceptions does not make the rule useless—quite the contrary. As with many rules, there are a few well-known violations.

choices.text: The rule must hold for every stable molecule, so violators cannot exist.
choices.why: Stable violators do exist: NO, for example, is a stable compound that violates the octet rule.

choices.text: The rule applies only to ionic compounds, not to covalent molecules.
choices.why: Covalent molecules such as F2 and CO2 follow the octet rule; the violations are particular types of covalent molecules.

explanation: As important and useful as the octet rule is, it has some well-known violations. As with many rules, there are exceptions, but that does not make the rule useless.

prompt: What makes a molecule an odd-electron molecule?

choices.text: The total number of valence electrons in the molecule is odd.
The molecule contains an odd number of atoms.
choices.why: The count that matters is electrons, not atoms. H2O has three atoms but 1 + 1 + 6 = 8 valence electrons, an even number.

choices.text: The central atom has an odd number of valence electrons.
choices.why: One atom's count is not enough. N has five valence electrons, but NH3 has 5 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 8 in total, an even number.

choices.text: The central atom makes an odd number of covalent bonds.
choices.why: The number of bonds doesn't decide it. P makes three bonds in PCl3, yet PCl3 has 5 + 7 + 7 + 7 = 26 valence electrons, an even number.

explanation: Add up the valence electrons of every atom in the molecule. If the total is odd, it is an odd-electron molecule, and at least one atom in it must violate the octet rule.

prompt: Why must at least one atom in a molecule with an odd number of valence electrons violate the octet rule?

choices.text: One electron is left unpaired, so the atom holding it has an odd number of electrons around it.
An odd number of electrons means the molecule must carry an electric charge.
choices.why: Odd-electron molecules such as NO and ClO2 are neutral. The violation comes from the unpaired electron, not from a charge.

choices.text: Odd-electron molecules always have more than eight electrons around the central atom.
choices.why: An odd total does not mean too many electrons around one atom. In NO, the atom holding the unpaired electron, N, has fewer than eight.

choices.text: Atoms in odd-electron molecules cannot share electrons, so they form no covalent bonds.
choices.why: Atoms in odd-electron molecules do share electrons; in NO, the N and O atoms share four electrons in a double bond.

explanation: Bonding pairs and lone pairs each hold two electrons, so an odd total cannot all be paired. The atom with the leftover electron has an odd number of electrons around it, so it cannot have exactly eight.

prompt: What is generally true of odd-electron molecules such as NO?

choices.text: They can be stable compounds, but most are very chemically reactive.
They are too unstable to exist and can never be isolated.
choices.why: NO is a stable compound. Having an odd number of electrons makes it very reactive, not impossible to isolate.

choices.text: They are unreactive, because the odd electron completes the valence shell.
choices.why: An odd number of electrons leaves at least one atom without an octet, and most odd-electron compounds are very reactive.

choices.text: They are very common; most molecules have an odd number of electrons.
choices.why: Stable odd-electron compounds are few. Most molecules have an even number of valence electrons.

explanation: Although they are few, some stable compounds have an odd number of valence electrons. NO is stable, but it is very chemically reactive, as are most other odd-electron compounds.

prompt: In NO, the N and O atoms share four electrons in a double bond. The O atom has two lone pairs, and the N atom has one lone pair plus one unpaired electron. How many electrons are around the N atom?
explanation: Count the shared electrons and N's own: 4 shared + 2 in the lone pair + 1 unpaired = 7. N falls short of an octet because NO has 5 + 6 = 11 valence electrons, an odd number.

prompt: Chlorine dioxide, ClO2, is used to bleach paper pulp and to disinfect drinking water. How many valence electrons does one ClO2 molecule have in total?
explanation: Cl has 7 valence electrons and each O has 6: 7 + 6 + 6 = 19. Because 19 is odd, ClO2 is an odd-electron molecule.

prompt: The hydroxyl radical, OH, is a neutral molecule made of one O atom and one H atom. It forms in the atmosphere and reacts with many pollutants. How many valence electrons does it have in total?
explanation: O has 6 valence electrons and H has 1: 6 + 1 = 7. The total is odd, so neutral OH is an odd-electron molecule, and like most odd-electron molecules it is very reactive.

prompt: Which of these species has an odd number of valence electrons? (A species shown without a charge is neutral.)

choices.text: NO3
NO3^−
choices.why: The 1− charge adds one electron: 5 + 3 × 6 + 1 = 24, an even number.

choices.text: N2O5
choices.why: Two N atoms give 2 × 5 = 10 and five O atoms give 5 × 6 = 30, for 40 valence electrons, an even number.

choices.text: HNO3
choices.why: H, N, and three O atoms give 1 + 5 + 3 × 6 = 24 valence electrons, an even number.

explanation: Neutral NO3 has 5 + 3 × 6 = 23 valence electrons. Because 23 is odd, at least one atom must violate the octet rule, so NO3 is an odd-electron molecule.

prompt: NO2 has 5 + 6 + 6 = 17 valence electrons. A student reasons, "17 is more than eight, so NO2 must be an expanded valence shell molecule." Which response is correct?

choices.text: 17 is the total for all three atoms; because 17 is odd, NO2 is an odd-electron molecule.
The student is right: any molecule with more than eight valence electrons has an expanded valence shell.
choices.why: Almost every molecule has more than eight valence electrons in total; CO2 has 16 and follows the octet rule. An expanded valence shell means more than eight electrons around one atom.

choices.text: The student is right: the N atom in NO2 has an expanded valence shell, like P in PF5.
choices.why: N is in the second row, so it cannot have more than eight electrons around it. Only central atoms in the third row or beyond, like P, can.

choices.text: NO2 follows the octet rule, because N is a second-row atom and cannot expand.
choices.why: Being in the second row keeps N from having more than eight electrons, but with an odd total of 17, not every atom in NO2 can have an octet.

explanation: The 17 electrons are spread over all three atoms; an expanded valence shell means more than eight around a single atom. Since 17 is odd, at least one atom must fall short of an octet, which makes NO2 an odd-electron molecule.

prompt: Which statement describes an electron-deficient molecule?

choices.text: A stable molecule in which an atom has fewer than eight electrons around it
A molecule that has an odd total number of valence electrons
choices.why: That describes an odd-electron molecule, such as NO.

choices.text: A molecule in which the central atom has more than eight electrons around it
choices.why: That describes an expanded valence shell molecule.

choices.text: A molecule that has lost electrons and so carries a positive charge
choices.why: A species that has lost electrons is a cation. Electron-deficient molecules are neutral; the term refers to how many electrons surround one atom.

explanation: Electron-deficient molecules are stable compounds that have fewer than eight electrons around an atom in the molecule.

prompt: The most common electron-deficient molecules are covalent compounds of which two elements?

choices.text: beryllium and boron
nitrogen and oxygen
choices.why: N and O usually reach octets, often by forming multiple bonds. When one of them lacks an octet, as N does in NO, it is because the molecule has an odd number of electrons.

choices.text: phosphorus and sulfur
choices.why: P and S, in the third row, are known for the opposite violation: they can have more than eight electrons around them.

choices.text: fluorine and chlorine
choices.why: F and Cl atoms bonded to a central atom have complete octets; in electron-deficient molecules, it is the central atom that is short of eight.

explanation: Beryllium commonly forms only two covalent bonds and boron only three, so in their covalent compounds the Be or B atom has fewer than eight electrons around it.

prompt: A student argues that H2O is an electron-deficient molecule because each H atom has only two electrons around it. What is wrong with this argument?

choices.text: Two electrons fill an H atom's valence shell, so each H atom in H2O is complete.
Each H atom in H2O actually has eight electrons around it.
choices.why: Each H atom shares one bonding pair with O, so it has two electrons around it, which is a full valence shell for H.

choices.text: The O atom, not H, is the atom short of electrons, with six around it.
choices.why: O shares two bonding pairs and has two lone pairs: 4 + 4 = 8 electrons, a complete octet.

choices.text: H2O is really an odd-electron molecule, not an electron-deficient one.
choices.why: H2O has 1 + 1 + 6 = 8 valence electrons, an even number, so it is not an odd-electron molecule.

explanation: An H atom needs only two electrons to fill its 1s subshell. In H2O each H atom has two electrons and the O atom has eight, so every atom has a full valence shell and H2O shows no violation of the octet rule.

prompt: Boron trichloride, BCl3, has 3 + 3 × 7 = 24 valence electrons, an even number. The B atom forms a single bond to each Cl atom, and each Cl atom has three lone pairs. How many electrons are around the B atom?
explanation: The three bonds use 6 electrons and the Cl lone pairs use 18, so all 24 are used and none are left for B. B has only 3 × 2 = 6 electrons around it: an even total does not guarantee an octet for every atom, and BCl3 is electron-deficient.

prompt: In both BF3 and NF3, the central atom forms a single bond to each of three F atoms. Which statement correctly compares the two molecules?

choices.text: B is left without an octet, but N has one because it also holds a lone pair.
Both central atoms lack an octet, so both molecules are electron-deficient.
choices.why: NF3 has two more valence electrons than BF3 (26 versus 24). They form a lone pair on N, which completes N's octet.

choices.text: Both central atoms have an octet, so both molecules follow the octet rule.
choices.why: All 24 of BF3's valence electrons are used in the three bonds and the F lone pairs, so B has only its three bonding pairs around it.

choices.text: N has more than eight electrons around it, so NF3 has an expanded valence shell.
choices.why: N is in the second row and cannot have more than eight electrons; three bonding pairs and one lone pair give it exactly eight.

explanation: BF3 has 3 + 3 × 7 = 24 valence electrons and NF3 has 5 + 3 × 7 = 26. In both, the three bonds and the F lone pairs use 24 electrons. B has nothing left over, so BF3 is electron-deficient, while N gets the last two electrons as a lone pair and has an octet.

prompt: Which of these molecules is electron-deficient?

choices.text: BeCl2
CO2
choices.why: C forms a double bond to each O atom, which gives it a complete octet, so CO2 follows the octet rule.

choices.text: OF2
choices.why: O forms two single bonds and keeps two lone pairs: 4 + 4 = 8 electrons, a complete octet.

choices.text: XeF2
choices.why: Xe, in the fifth row, has more than eight electrons around it in XeF2, so XeF2 is an expanded valence shell molecule.

explanation: In BeCl2, the Be atom forms only two covalent bonds and has no lone pairs, so it has fewer than eight electrons around it. BeCl2 is an electron-deficient molecule.

prompt: Which central atoms can form expanded valence shell molecules, with more than eight electrons around them?

choices.text: Only atoms in the third row of the periodic table or beyond
Any atom with five or more valence electrons
choices.why: N and O have five and six valence electrons, but they are in the second row, so they cannot have more than eight electrons around them.

choices.text: Only atoms in the second row of the periodic table
choices.why: This reverses the rule. Second-row atoms such as C, N, and O are limited to eight electrons; atoms in the third row or beyond, such as P and S, can expand.

choices.text: Only atoms of noble gases, such as Xe
choices.why: Xe can have an expanded valence shell, but so can atoms of other elements in the third row or beyond, such as P and S.

explanation: Expanded valence shell molecules are formed only by central atoms in the third row of the periodic table or beyond. Second-row atoms such as N and O are limited to eight electrons.

prompt: PCl5 is a stable compound in which P forms five covalent bonds, but NCl5 does not exist, even though N, like P, has five valence electrons. Which statement best explains this?

choices.text: N is in the second row; its n = 2 valence shell has only 2s and 2p subshells, which hold at most eight electrons.
N has too few valence electrons to form five covalent bonds.
choices.why: N has five valence electrons, the same as P, and P does form five bonds in PCl5. The limit is how many electrons N's valence shell can hold.

choices.text: NCl5 would have an odd number of valence electrons.
choices.why: NCl5 would have 5 + 5 × 7 = 40 valence electrons, an even number. The problem is the number of electrons that would surround N.

choices.text: Cl atoms can form only one covalent bond each.
choices.why: Each Cl forms just one bond in PCl5 too, so this doesn't rule out NCl5; the N atom can't hold the electrons that five bonds require.

explanation: Five single bonds would put 5 × 2 = 10 electrons around N. Expanded valence shells occur only for central atoms in the third row or beyond; N is in the second row, and its n = 2 shell (2s and 2p) holds at most eight electrons.

prompt: If each of these molecules existed, its central atom would be bonded to four F atoms and have more than eight electrons around it. Which one is not expected to exist?

choices.text: OF4
SF4
choices.why: S is in the third row, so it can have more than eight electrons around it; SF4 is a known compound.

choices.text: SeF4
choices.why: Se is in the fourth row, so it can have more than eight electrons around it; SeF4 is a known compound.

choices.text: XeF4
choices.why: Xe is in the fifth row, so it can have more than eight electrons around it; XeF4 is a known compound.

explanation: Only central atoms in the third row of the periodic table or beyond can have expanded valence shells. O is in the second row, so it cannot have more than eight electrons around it, and OF4 is not expected to exist.

prompt: Which of these molecules is an expanded valence shell molecule?

choices.text: IF5
SCl2
choices.why: S is in the third row and could expand, but in SCl2 it forms two single bonds and has two lone pairs: exactly eight electrons.

choices.text: CF4
choices.why: C forms four single bonds, which gives it exactly eight electrons; C is a second-row atom and cannot expand.

choices.text: NO
choices.why: NO has 5 + 6 = 11 valence electrons, an odd number, so it is an odd-electron molecule. N and O are second-row atoms and cannot expand.

explanation: In IF5, the I atom forms five single bonds, which alone put 5 × 2 = 10 electrons around it, more than eight. I is in the fifth row, so it can have an expanded valence shell.

prompt: In a certain molecule, the central atom forms four single bonds and also has one lone pair. Which statement about the central atom is correct?

choices.text: It has an expanded valence shell, with 10 electrons around it.
It follows the octet rule, with eight electrons around it.
choices.why: Four single bonds hold 4 × 2 = 8 electrons, and the lone pair adds 2 more, for 10 in all.

choices.text: It is electron-deficient, with five electrons around it.
choices.why: Each bond and the lone pair is a pair of electrons, not a single electron: 4 × 2 + 2 = 10.

choices.text: It has nine electrons around it: eight in bonds plus one in the lone pair.
choices.why: A lone pair is two electrons, not one, so the count is 8 + 2 = 10.

explanation: Each single bond is a shared pair and the lone pair is another pair, so the central atom has 4 × 2 + 2 = 10 electrons around it. More than eight is an expanded valence shell, so the central atom must be in the third row or beyond.

prompt: In PF5, the P atom forms a single bond to each of five F atoms, and each F atom has three lone pairs. A student says the F atoms are the ones that violate the octet rule. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Each F atom has eight electrons; the P atom, with 10, is the one that violates the rule.
Each F atom has 10 electrons around it, so the student is right.
choices.why: Each F atom shares one bonding pair with P and has three lone pairs: 2 + 6 = 8, a complete octet.

choices.text: No atom violates the rule, because the P atom has exactly eight electrons.
choices.why: Five single bonds put 5 × 2 = 10 electrons around P, which is more than eight.

choices.text: The P atom has only five electrons around it, so PF5 is electron-deficient.
choices.why: Each of P's five bonds is a shared pair, so P has 5 × 2 = 10 electrons around it, not five.

explanation: Each F atom has one bonding pair and three lone pairs, a complete octet. The P atom has five bonding pairs, so it has 10 electrons in its valence shell, which makes PF5 an expanded valence shell molecule.

prompt: Sulfur hexafluoride, SF6, is used as an insulating gas in high-voltage electrical equipment. The S atom forms a single bond to each of the six F atoms and has no lone pairs. How many electrons are around the S atom?
explanation: Six single bonds hold 6 × 2 = 12 electrons around S. That is more than eight, so SF6 is an expanded valence shell molecule, which S can form because it is in the third row.

prompt: In XeF2, the Xe atom forms a single bond to each F atom, each F atom has three lone pairs, and all remaining valence electrons go on Xe as lone pairs. How many electrons are around the Xe atom?
explanation: XeF2 has 8 + 7 + 7 = 22 valence electrons. The two bonds use 4 and the F lone pairs use 12, leaving 6 (three lone pairs) on Xe, so Xe has 4 + 6 = 10 electrons around it, an expanded valence shell.

prompt: Like the N atom in NF3, the Cl atom in ClF3 forms a single bond to each of three F atoms. Each F atom has three lone pairs, and all remaining valence electrons go on Cl as lone pairs. How many electrons are around the Cl atom?
explanation: ClF3 has 7 + 3 × 7 = 28 valence electrons. The three bonds use 6 and the F lone pairs use 18, leaving 4 (two lone pairs) on Cl, so Cl has 6 + 4 = 10 electrons around it. Unlike N, Cl is in the third row, so it can have an expanded valence shell.
